previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of fibrosing mesenteritis, recurrent partial small bowel obstructions, and chronic GI dysmotility, was admitted for abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and dehydration after an episode of bilious emesis. CT imaging showed no acute intra-abdominal process or obstruction, with findings unchanged from prior studies. She was managed conservatively with bowel rest, IV fluids, and symptom control. Her elevated creatinine improved from prerenal acute kidney injury, and leukocytosis resolved with hydration. INR was transiently elevated and managed by holding warfarin temporarily. She advanced from NPO to full liquids and soft solids, with pain controlled on oral medications. Misoprostol was increased to 200mcg four times daily, and pregabalin dosing was adjusted. She was discharged home with instructions for continued oral intake, IV fluids as needed, and close follow-up.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ with fibrosing mesenteritis, recurrent partial SBO, HCV, DVT 
on coumadin, and multiple hospitalizations for abdominal pain 
admitted with persistent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting x 
1d, similar to prior admissions.  
.  
## NOTE: for future admissions please give IV toradol (per 
chronic pain service) and avoid IV narcotics as much as possible 
for pain control as the narcotics exacerbate the pt's n/v. also 
please do not perform any more abd CT scans (per attending) 
unless high suspicion for acute abdomen.
.
# Abdominal pain: Pain consistent with her typical flare 
requiring admission. Namely, when the patient is at home, she 
has nausea/vomitting due to abdominal pain which she then treats 
with her prescribed opioids, thus further worsening her 
nausea/vomitting. She then becomes dehydrated and is admitted 
for pain/nausea/vomittng control. During this admission as in 
the past, her KUB was without acute process. Importantly, there 
are specific attending orders for no future abdominal CT scans 
unless very acute clinical picture. Upon admission the patient 
was made NPO, and aggressive IV fluids were started with IV 
narcotics and IV phenergan. The patient improved in terms of her 
abdominal sx and nausea; however, on the morning of her 
admission to the medicine floor she triggered for a systolic BP 
in the 70-80s with HR in ___. The patient complained of slight 
dizziness but was otherwise clinically stable. Her narcotics 
were held and she was given aggressive IV fluids with response. 
This episode was thought to be due to narcotics. The patient 
subsequently responded well and was resumed on her home PO pain 
meds (Morphine SR 30q12h, Morphine liq ___ q4hprn) and PO 
phenergan. She was also continued on her home PO misoprostol and 
lyrica. The chronic pain service was consulted and recommended 
that she continue her home pain meds, consider changing lyrica 
to neurontin if patient believes that it works better, consider 
lidoderm patches up to 3 for 12 hrs on, 12 hr off, and 
importantly that providers can use IV toradol during future 
acute episodes/hospitalizations rather than IV narcotics which 
would worsen her nausea/vomitting and lead to cardiorespiratory 
depression. They also agreed with use of methylnaltrexone if the 
patient's GI physician (Dr. ___ believes that this will be 
helpful. The patient will followup with the pain service as an 
outpatient next week.
.  
# Anemia: On admission HCT was 38, which then dropped to 30.6, 
with concurrent decrease in WBC and Plt count. During this time 
pt also triggered with hypotension with HR in ___, which was 
probably secondary to high levels of narcotics. After ruling out 
hemolysis with labwork, this anemia was most consistent with 
dilutional effect in setting of aggressive IV fluid repletion. 
Her HCT was stable around ___ for the rest of admission.
.  
# h/o DVT on coumadin: INR was therapeutic during admission. We 
continued her home coumadin. 
.  
# Hypothyroidism: no active issues. we continued her home 
levothyroxine  
.
